left_defects.translation: capable of excuse / it was read with patience

right_defects.translation: capable of excuse / was read with patience

why: Both render the repeated catchword patiens twice; the rest of the crossing is equally faithful.
Both mishandle the carried-over hin at the break in the same way; otherwise equivalent.

right_defects.translation: nonetheless great thanks to you ... (no verb)
alone among the others, carried our goods safely

why: Left completes the sentence that crosses the break (gratiam habuissem ... gessisti); right leaves a verbless fragment and adds a bridging ellipsis.

left_defects.source: scio enim ... suo piculo se absoluere. Ad si res ... Vale
left_defects.translation: proverb content and rest of the letter dropped

left_defects.source: si maiorem de maioribus tuis ... rationem habueris
left_defects.translation: if you take more account of your own virtues

right_defects.source: diligendis nulla de me ratio habita fuerit. scio enim ... Vale
right_defects.translation: in whom... (entire end of letter dropped)

right_defects.source: a meipsum et item alios ... preter bonum et equum sustinuisse
right_defects.translation: other citizens ... similarly stripped of their rights, even though they had sustained the good and the fair

why: Both drop the end of the letter that crosses the break, but right drops more, including the crossing clause itself.

left_defects.source: angelica / protectione prohiberentur. Sicut refert cirillus ... dicens.
left_defects.translation: if the angelic / [jumps to Behold, I am given]

right_defects.source: angelica / protectione prohiberentur. Sicut refert cirillus ... dicens.
right_defects.translation: if angelic / [jumps to Behold, I am given]

why: Both drop the same large passage across the break; remaining differences are minor.

left_defects.source: qua recipe / reculabant inherentes legalibus ceremoniis
left_defects.translation: which he was receiving / they were rejecting the legal ceremonies of Moses

right_defects.translation: By no means do I say this; rather

why: Left inverts the meaning of the crossing clause (receiving/rejecting); right keeps clinging to the ceremonies correct and only drops refused to receive.
Differences are a leftover catchword and small word choices; right reads cleaner across the break.
Both carry fides unicum est os / et instrumentum across the break faithfully.

left_defects.source: tibi celesti sponso desponsare voluisti. z hodie corpus z sanguinem tuum ad donum noue desponsationis ... ptulisti
left_defects.translation: who in the laver of baptism / Blessed are You, most generous God

why: Left drops the completion of the crossing sentence (betrothal clause); right renders it.

left_defects.translation: dwelling place of the holy ones of God

right_defects.translation: dwelling place of the holy of holies

why: Both mistranslate the phrase completing the crossing sentence in comparable ways.

left_defects.source: [Domine] tui qui causam doloris mei assumpsisti
left_defects.translation: I, who have taken up the cause of my sorrow

why: Left turns the address to Christ (You who took up) into a first-person clause in the sentence leading to the break; the crossing itself is handled the same.

left_defects.source: sanguinem suum / non dubitauerunt fundere ... Confessorum ... virginum ... Amen

right_defects.source: sanguinem suum / non dubitauerunt fundere ... Confessorum ... virginum ... Amen

why: Both drop the rest of the litany after the break identically.
The break falls between prayers and both render both sides faithfully.
Both duplicate the catchword est; otherwise equivalent.
Break falls between versicles and both render the adjacent sentences faithfully (right lacks the opening line, far from the break).
Break falls at a paragraph boundary; both render it cleanly with minor flaws elsewhere.
